summary: Discusses strategies for assigning the existing IP address space in ways that conserve it and slow the explosive growth of routing tables. It helped lead to classless addressing, and was replaced by RFC 1519.

eli5.summary: Instead of keeping a separate list entry for every street, you group many neighbors together under one entry. Supernetting does that to Internet addresses so routers have shorter lists.

subtitle: Organizing network addresses to reduce routing table growth.

tldr.problem: Internet routing tables were growing exponentially and the class-B address space was becoming exhausted, threatening the scalability of Internet routing.
tldr.mechanism: Allocate large blocks of Class-C addresses to service providers, who then sub-allocate to customers. Route aggregation allows multiple networks to be advertised as a single supernet using a network mask.
tldr.outcome: This approach dramatically slowed routing table growth from 150% annually to about 6% when implemented with classless routing protocols. It was a bridge solution until IPv6 was deployed.

today: RFC 1338 was obsoleted by RFC 1519, which provided a more refined description of CIDR. The supernetting model became the foundation of modern IP address allocation and remains in use today through CIDR, where addresses are allocated hierarchically and routing tables are aggregated.

sections.title: The Scaling Problem
sections.content:
By 1992, the Internet faced three serious scaling problems: exhaustion of Class-B network addresses, explosive growth of routing tables in core routers, and eventual exhaustion of the 32-bit IP address space. The RFC focuses on the first two as urgent short-term problems expected to become critical within one to three years.

The core issue was that Class-C networks were too small for medium-sized organizations (254 hosts), while Class-B networks (65,534 hosts) were too large. Organizations in the 200-4,000 host range had to request multiple Class-C networks, and every network needed its own routing table entry, causing exponential growth. Routing tables in default-free routers contained about 4,700 entries and were doubling roughly every 10 months.
sections.eli5: The Internet was running out of medium-sized address blocks, so instead organizations got many tiny blocks. This made every router keep track of thousands of different paths, and the problem was getting worse every month.

sections.title: The Supernetting Solution
sections.content:
Supernetting has two components: distributed address allocation and route aggregation. The plan allocates large contiguous blocks of Class-C network numbers (typically 2,048 networks, or a /13 prefix) to network service providers. Service providers then allocate smaller blocks from their space to customer organizations using a network mask to specify the address range.

The key innovation is that multiple customer networks can be advertised as a single aggregate route. For example, a provider with 2,048 Class-C networks (192.24.0.0 through 192.31.255.0) can advertise one aggregate route (192.24.0.0/255.248.0.0) instead of 2,048 separate routes, as long as the networks are contiguous and topologically connected through the provider.

However, aggregation has limitations. Organizations with multiple connections (multi-homed sites) must still advertise their networks explicitly from all providers. When a site changes providers, the old provider's aggregate has a hole that must be filled with an explicit route. These cases prevent complete aggregation efficiency.
sections.eli5: A service provider gets a large block of addresses and splits it among customers. Instead of telling every router about every customer separately, the provider says one simple thing: all these thousands of addresses come through me. That works as long as you make sure the group is connected through one path.

sections.title: Changes to Routing Protocols
sections.content:
The existing interdomain routing protocol at the time, EGP and early BGP versions, used class-based routing where every network was assumed to be Class-A, Class-B, or Class-C. Supernetting requires two fundamental changes: the concept of network class must be deprecated, and routers must perform routing based on longest-match, where a packet is sent via the route with the most specific (longest) network mask that matches the destination.

The RFC establishes two rules for route advertisement. First, multi-homed networks must always be advertised explicitly by every provider they connect through, even if they are part of a provider's supernet aggregate. Second, a router performing aggregation must discard packets that match the aggregate but not any explicit routes within it. This prevents routing loops when a customer's address space is advertised as part of a provider's aggregate, but the customer is temporarily unreachable.

The implementation requires preconfigured address ranges in border routers. Rather than dynamically discovering what to aggregate, routers are manually configured with the address blocks to aggregate. This gives operators precise control and prevents mistakes from temporary unreachability of networks.
sections.eli5: Routers need new rules: longest path wins (most specific address range), and you must announce multi-homed places every time, even if they're part of someone's group. You tell routers what to group by hand, because asking them to figure it out automatically doesn't always work.

sections.title: Impact on Routing Table Growth
sections.content:
The analysis in the RFC projects dramatic effects on routing table growth. In 1992, the default-free routing table (such as NSFNET backbone routers) contained approximately 4,700 entries. Without intervention, assuming 150% annual growth, routing tables could exceed 75,000 entries within three years. Under the supernetting plan with 100 service providers and adoption by 90% of them, the same period would see routing tables grow to only about 13,145 entries.

This reduction comes from aggregation: instead of multiple Class-C networks per customer producing multiple routes, a provider advertises one supernet. The RFC estimates fewer than 100 multi-homed organizations at the time, growing to roughly 800 in three years. The dominant growth factor becomes multi-homed routes (800) plus provider routes (100) plus yearly additions for new providers (50 per year), totaling a 6% annual growth rate instead of 150%.

The RFC emphasizes that the benefit depends on deploying both the new addressing plan and routing protocols that support classless destinations. Without the protocols, merely allocating addresses hierarchically provides no routing reduction. Initial deployments could see temporary rapid routing table growth as the new addressing plan spreads before new routing protocol support is deployed.
sections.eli5: Without supernetting, routers would need to keep track of thousands of new addresses every few months. With supernetting and new routing software, growth slows down dramatically. The improvement only works if both the new address plan and new routing software are deployed together.

sections.title: Implementation and Legacy
sections.content:
RFC 1338 was a proposal for the short-to-medium term while the Internet community worked on longer-term solutions like IPv6. The approach was adopted: service providers did receive large address blocks, routers were updated to support classless interdomain routing (CIDR), and routing became based on network+mask pairs. This allowed the Internet to continue functioning throughout the 1990s despite the predicted explosion in routing table size.

The RFC was obsoleted by RFC 1519, which provided a more refined description of CIDR. The supernetting model established by RFC 1338 became the foundation of modern IP address allocation: today, addresses are allocated hierarchically from IANA to regional registries to service providers to end-users, and routing aggregation remains a core principle. The shift from classful to classless routing was complete by the mid-1990s.
sections.eli5: This idea worked: providers got big blocks, routers learned to group addresses, and the Internet could keep growing. It was supposed to be temporary while people built IPv6, but it worked so well that it's still how things work today.
